title: How to Create a High-Probability Retirement Plan Using Monte Carlo Simulations
description: Moving beyond 'Average Returns' to stress-test your future.
content:
Standard retirement calculators use linear math: 'If I earn 7% every year, I will have $2 Million.' But the market doesn't earn 7% every year. It earns +20%, -15%, +5%. The sequence of these returns matters. **Monte Carlo Simulation** is a statistical tool that runs 10,000 different random market scenarios (Good times, Bad times, Great Depression 2.0) to determine the *probability* of your money lasting. This guide explains how to use this tool to find a 'Success Rate' you can trust.

Key Takeaways

  • The Flaw of Averages: Average returns hide failure risks. If you retire into a bear market, you might run out of money even if the 30-year average return is good. Monte Carlo accounts for this 'Sequence Risk'.
  • Target Probability: You don't need 100% success (that requires saving too much). Most planners aim for 90-95% success. This means in 9,000 out of 10,000 simulated futures, you die with money.
  • The 'Failures' are Fixable: A 'Failure' in a simulation usually means running out of money at age 92. In reality, you would adjust spending at age 70 if the market crashed. Simulations assume you are a robot who never adjusts.
  • Tools: Free tools like 'Portfolio Visualizer', 'FIRECalc', or 'Empower' allow you to run these simulations yourself.

Why It Matters (US Context)

Monte Carlo is the industry standard for financial planning. It helps answer 'Am I safe?' better than a simple spreadsheet. It models inflation shocks, deflation, and crashes simultaneously.

Reading the Results

You run the sim. It says '85% Success'. What now?

Interpreting the Score

  • >95%: You are over-saved. Spend more. Retire earlier.
  • 80-95%: The Sweet Spot. You are likely fine. You might need to cut spending slightly in a worst-case scenario.
  • <75%: Danger. You are relying on luck (a bull market). You need to save more, work longer, or spend less.

How to Improve the Score

Variable 1: Spending. Cutting annual spend by $5,000 often boosts success by 10%.
Variable 2: Flexibility. Checking the box for 'I will cut spending if portfolio drops' usually jumps success to 99%.
Variable 3: Asset Allocation. Moving from 100% stocks to 60/40 often improves success because it reduces the depth of the crashes in the bad scenarios.

Using the Tool

  1. Input Conservative Data: Assume Social Security is cut by 25%. Assume you live to 95. If the model survives this stress test, you are solid.
  2. Run Every Year: Monte Carlo is a snapshot. Run it every January. If your score drops below 80%, make adjustments (spend less that year). If it stays above 90%, enjoy your life.
  3. Don't Obsess: It is a model, not a crystal ball. It can't predict World War III. It just predicts that your plan is robust based on historical norms.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is FIRECalc good?

Yes, it's a classic. It uses historical backtesting (what actually happened) rather than Monte Carlo (random variations). Both are useful. Backtesting shows 'What if I retired in 1929?'. Monte Carlo shows 'What if the future is worse than 1929?'

Why not aim for 100%?

To get 100%, you would have to work 5 extra years or live on rice. The 'utility cost' of that safety is too high. Accept small risk and be flexible.

Does it account for taxes?

Basic calculators don't. Advanced ones (NewRetirement) do. Taxes are a major expense. Ensure you are modeling 'After-Tax' spending capacity.
